useInsteadWhen.condition: The user wants the reported smell actually fixed rather than reported.

useInsteadWhen.condition: The goal is to find exploitable or quality defects to fix, not to characterize the change.

useInsteadWhen.condition: The architectural decision the ADR would record has not been made yet.

useInsteadWhen.condition: A production service is degraded or down right now with users affected — mitigate there first, then hand root cause back here.
The code is behaving as designed but is too slow or too memory-hungry.
No failure has been observed and the user wants code read for latent defects.

matrix.scope: Gets a specific change from merged to fully released and back out again: rollout strategy, flag plan, expand-contract migration, release checklist and go/no-go, tested rollback, DORA measurement. Owns the window from deploy start to bake complete.

Nothing exists yet — the project must be scoped, planned and built before there is anything to release.

matrix.scope: Responds to a DECLARED, live, user-impacting failure: severity triage, roles and comms, mitigate before diagnosing, reproduction harness, timeline, blameless postmortem/CoE. Episodic and novel by definition.

Service is already restored and the remaining work is finding the root cause.
The mitigation is a redeploy or rollback and the question is how to execute it safely.
The retrospective is over a diff rather than over an outage.

useInsteadWhen.condition: An incident is declared, or the condition exceeds what any existing runbook covers.
The service is not yet built and the SLO targets are being chosen for the first time.
A rollout is actively in flight and has not finished baking.
The autonomous loop's subject is the repository and its output is a pull request.

matrix.scope: Authors a skill directory for this plugin — router, references, standards shelf and workflow template — that passes scripts/validate.mjs.

the deliverable is prose for a human reader rather than a skill directory under .claude/skills/

useInsteadWhen.condition: The ask stops at the plan — a task DAG with routing — rather than conducting the build to a shipped v1.
The unit of work is one already-scoped task needing one workflow, not a whole project spanning phases.

matrix.scope: Engineers the information an agent carries at runtime: context budgets/placement, compaction with an addressable store, typed shared state with merge rules and checkpoints between phases, supersession of stale facts, and trace invariants; deliverable is a context/state design or an evidence-confirmed audit.

useInsteadWhen.condition: The subject is what Claude is PERMITTED to do — permissions, hooks, MCP servers, schedules — not the information it carries.

The subject is a product's persistent data model or database schema, not an agent's runtime state.
The deliverable is prose for a human reader rather than a context/state contract or audit.

matrix.description: Engineer what an agent carries at runtime: context budgets and placement, compaction paired with an addressable store, typed shared state with per-field merge rules and checkpoints handed between workflow phases, supersession of stale facts, and property-based invariants over agent traces. Use when the user asks to manage or debug agent context or agent memory, decide what to keep, compact, or evict, design the state passed between agents or phases, fix an agent that forgets, repeats itself, or acts on a stale fact, or verify that compaction lost nothing that mattered. The subject is the information an agent carries while it runs. For Claude's own configuration — permissions, hooks, MCP servers, schedules — use loop-harness. For the orchestration shapes that execute (pipeline, parallel, guarded loops), use loop-engine. For a product's database schema or data model, use loop-design. For prose a human reads, use loop-docs.

matrix.scope: Understands code that already exists: recovers the as-built architecture from evidence, traces feature flows end to end, builds onboarding dossiers, and reverse-engineers ADRs for unrecorded decisions; deliverable is an evidence-anchored, dated dossier/map/trace with a coverage statement — descriptive, never a diff.
matrix.description: Understand an existing codebase and recover what was never written down: map the as-built architecture from code, trace how a feature actually flows end to end, build an onboarding dossier for an unfamiliar repo, and reverse-engineer ADRs for decisions the record never captured — every claim anchored to a file:line. Use when the user asks how a codebase or subsystem works, to explain or map an unfamiliar repo, to trace a feature or request path, to onboard onto a project, or to recover why the code is the way it is. The subject is code that already exists. For designing a system or making a new architecture decision, use loop-design. For turning findings into maintained documentation that ships in the repo, use loop-docs. For the impact and risk of a specific change set or diff, use loop-audit. For explaining one observed defective behavior, use loop-debug.

useInsteadWhen.condition: The architecture or decision is being made now, for code not yet written — not read out of code that already runs.
The deliverable is a maintained document that ships in the repo (README, guide, ADR prose kept current) rather than a dated comprehension dossier.
The subject is a specific change set, diff, PR, or release — not the codebase as it stands.
There is one observed defective behavior to explain, not a system to understand.

matrix.scope: The front door: converts a situation described in the user’s own words — no skill named, deliverable unclear — into a justified routing verdict (single skill, ordered chain, or escalation), then dispatches and conducts the handoffs; does no domain work; deliverable is the verdict with its because-lines plus the routing note.
matrix.description: Route a request to the right Heimdall skill when the developer does not know which one fits: a short discriminating interview, classification on the boundary audit's checkable questions, a routing verdict naming the skill or the ordered chain — each pick justified by the one-line answer that selected it — then delegated invocation with managed handoffs. Use when the user asks which skill to use, describes a situation without naming a deliverable, wants Heimdall to decide and drive, or arrives at the plugin's front door with 'help me with this'. This skill does no domain work; its deliverable is the verdict and the dispatch. For planning an already-named multi-phase job into a task DAG with model routing, use loop-orchestrate. For conducting a whole project brief to a shipped v1, use loop-build. For a capability no existing skill covers, use loop-skill.

useInsteadWhen.condition: The job is already named and scoped and what is wanted is a multi-phase plan — a task DAG with model routing and a cost ledger — not a decision about which skill applies.
The user wants a whole project conducted brief-to-v1 (or the chain has grown to ~5 hops) — conducting needs gates, repair rounds, and a ledger, which guide deliberately does not have.
No existing skill’s boundary contains the ask — the deliverable is a new skill, not a route among existing ones.

matrix.scope: Conducts a venture idea through the whole product lifecycle — discovery, vision/roadmap with a kill-pivot-proceed gate, go-to-market, build plan, deploy plan, operate plan — as verified decision documents with human gates; produces the brief loop-build starts from, never code.

useInsteadWhen.condition: The brief already exists (or the product decisions are made) and the ask is to conduct engineering to a shipped v1.
The decomposition wanted is of agent work into a task DAG with routing, not of a venture into lifecycle decisions.
The ask is one cited question with no lifecycle attached — loop-venture's nodes delegate their evidence gathering there.
The ask is a reuse/adapt/build verdict on one named capability rather than the whole venture's shape.
The user cannot yet name the deliverable at all — route first; venture conduct starts once the ask is a product/service idea.

matrix.scope: Runs an empirical study whose evidence the agent GENERATES rather than gathers: falsifiable hypothesis, harness with independently captured ground truth, executed run, then a re-derivation/mutation/confound gate before any number is reported. Deliverable is a reproducible finding, not a cited answer and not shipped code.

useInsteadWhen.condition: The answer already exists in sources and the work is finding and verifying it. Checkable: does answering require executing something that does not exist yet, or reading something that does?
There is a named component whose mechanism is being chosen from a known answer space. loop-algo benchmarks candidates; loop-experiment tests a hypothesis that could simply be false.
A failure was already observed and the question is why. loop-experiment's subject has not failed — it is being measured.
The deliverable is an automated correctness test that lives in the repo, not a one-off study producing a finding.
The subject is a change set whose risk and blast radius need assessing, rather than a hypothesis needing measurement.

overlaps.risk: loop-design/references/deployment.md (149 lines) already IS loop-ship's entire declared scope: rolling/blue-green/canary with mechanics and failure modes, the risk→strategy table, the four feature-flag kinds and hygiene, expand-contract migrations, IaC, CI/CD gates, tested rollback, and the full DORA section. loop-design's current description explicitly advertises 'deployment strategy' and 'plan a deployment or rollout strategy' as trigger phrases. Shipping loop-ship without moving that content creates two skills with identical knowledge and colliding triggers, and whichever wins the match is arbitrary.
overlaps.resolution: This is a content migration, not a wording fix, and it is the single highest-value action in Phase 2. Move deployment.md out of loop-design into loop-ship (split as references/rollout-strategies.md + references/migrations.md + references/dora.md), leaving behind a ~15-line design-time stub in loop-design that states only 'pick the coarse delivery shape and record it as an ADR; the execution machinery lives in loop-ship' plus the pointer. Remove 'deployment strategy'/'plan a deployment or rollout strategy' from loop-design's description (done in the rewrite). loop-design step 6 shrinks to an ADR-emitting decision; loop-ship owns everything from deploy start to bake complete. If Construction declines this migration, loop-ship must NOT ship as a separate skill — it would be a duplicate of loop-design/references/deployment.md.

overlaps.risk: loop-design/references/nfr.md already owns SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerting ('multi-window, multi-burn-rate', 'alert on SLO burn, not causes'), the three observability pillars, RED/USE/golden signals, and OpenTelemetry — which the plan assigns to loop-operate as 'SLI/SLO/error budgets, alert design'. Both would answer 'what should my SLOs be?' and 'how do I make this observable?'.
overlaps.resolution: Split nfr.md on the design-time/run-time seam. loop-design keeps target SETTING: the intake table, availability math, RTO/RPO, scalability axis, cost, build-vs-buy, and the pre-sign-off checklist — everything answered before launch with no telemetry in hand. Move the SLI/SLO/error-budget MEASUREMENT half plus the entire observability section into loop-operate/references/slo-and-alerting.md and observability.md, and have loop-design's nfr.md cross-reference it the same way it already cross-references loop-review for threat modeling. Test of the seam: if the answer requires reading a live metric, it belongs to loop-operate.

overlaps.risk: Both are triggered by 'production is unhealthy'. An alert firing is genuinely ambiguous between them, and both plausibly claim auto-rollback (loop-operate has 'SLO-gated auto-rollback', loop-incident has 'mitigate-before-diagnose'). This is the thinnest boundary in the 18 and the most likely mis-selection at runtime.
overlaps.resolution: Separate on a checkable predicate, not a vibe, and state it as the first sentence of BOTH SKILL.md bodies: 'Does a runbook exist for this condition AND does executing it restore the SLI?' Yes → loop-operate (steady state, no declaration). No, or impact exceeds the runbook's scope, or a human must be paged/coordinated → loop-incident. Corollary: loop-operate owns AUTOMATED mitigation of KNOWN conditions; loop-incident owns HUMAN-COORDINATED mitigation of NOVEL ones, and only loop-incident writes postmortems. Merge tripwire for the verify-sweep in Phase 2: if either SKILL.md ends up spending more than ~30% of its body restating the other's phase, they are not separable and should be merged into loop-operate with an explicit 'incident mode' section — better one honest skill than two that fight for the same trigger.

overlaps.risk: 'Rollback plan' (loop-ship) and 'SLO-gated auto-rollback' (loop-operate) name the same action, and both claim canary. A user asking 'roll this back' matches both.
overlaps.resolution: Split on mechanism vs trigger, and on rollout lifecycle. loop-ship AUTHORS the rollback mechanism and proves it works (the button); loop-operate OWNS THE SIGNAL that presses it unattended (the wire from burn rate to the button) and the autonomy level at which it may fire. Temporal rule: from deploy start until bake completes, the rollout belongs to loop-ship; after bake, the service belongs to loop-operate. Canary appears in both but at different granularity — loop-ship defines the ramp schedule and abort criteria, loop-operate supplies the SLI those criteria are evaluated against.

overlaps.risk: loop-debug's current description claims 'a crash', 'unexpected behavior', and 'asks why something is broken' — which is exactly what a user says during an outage. loop-debug will hijack incident triggers and start bisecting while the service is down, which is precisely the failure mode loop-incident exists to prevent (mitigate before diagnose).
overlaps.resolution: Split on service impact, not on symptom vocabulary. loop-incident requires a LIVE, USER-IMPACTING failure; loop-debug requires a REPRODUCIBLE DEFECT with no restoration obligation. Both descriptions must carry the pointer explicitly (done in the rewrites) and loop-debug's SKILL.md §1 must open with the interrupt: 'if a production service is currently degraded with users affected, stop and use loop-incident first.' The plan's handoff chain already encodes the correct order — the descriptions must encode it too, because selection happens before either body is read.

overlaps.risk: loop-review/references/quality-checks.md already covers dead/duplicated code and maintainability, and loop-review's current description advertises 'code-quality or best-practices review'. loop-pattern's declared scope (SOLID, Fowler smells, idioms) is the remediation of exactly those findings. 'Clean up this code' and 'is this idiomatic?' match both.
overlaps.resolution: Split on the artifact produced, which is unambiguous at request time: loop-review emits a FINDINGS LIST and touches no code; loop-pattern emits a DIFF. Keep quality-checks.md in loop-review (detection is a review job) but add a 'remediation' column pointing each smell class at loop-pattern's catalog entry, so the two compose instead of competing. loop-review's description must gain the explicit clause 'it judges, it does not refactor' (done in the rewrite) — that single clause is what keeps 'clean up this code' out of it.

overlaps.risk: Both are autonomous loops with an autonomy ladder, and the plan says loop-operate 'carries the autonomy dial wired to loop-autopilot's ladder'. If both define the ladder, the two definitions drift and 'how much should this fix itself?' matches both. Separately, loop-autopilot's SCALE rung (canary-merge.workflow.js) already specifies merge-behind-canary + agent-driven rollback — loop-ship + loop-operate content living inside loop-autopilot.
overlaps.resolution: Separable on subject and are worth keeping apart — autopilot's subject is the repository and its output is a draft PR; operate's subject is a running service and its output is a mitigated SLI — but the SHARED ladder needs exactly one home. Recommend promoting the OBSERVE→VERIFY→…→SCALE ladder to loop-engine/references/autonomy-ladder.md and having BOTH loop-autopilot and loop-operate cite it; neither redefines it. Additionally, canary-merge.workflow.js should cite loop-ship for the rollout mechanism and loop-operate for the SLO gate rather than restating them.

overlaps.risk: 'What's the best way to do X in React?' is genuinely ambiguous — it could mean 'which library' (scout) or 'which idiom' (pattern).
overlaps.resolution: Disambiguate on the dependency manifest, a fact both skills can check in one command: if answering the question adds a line to package.json/requirements.txt/go.mod, it is loop-scout; if the dependency is already there, it is loop-pattern. State this test in both descriptions ('already in the project' vs 'not yet adopted') and in loop-pattern's SKILL.md §1.

overlaps.risk: 'Should this be sharded?', 'is this fast enough?', and 'how should this queue work?' plausibly match both; loop-design/references/backend.md already discusses sharding and access patterns.
overlaps.resolution: Split on granularity with a concrete test: if the deliverable is a box-and-arrow diagram, a contract, or a deployable topology → loop-design. If the deliverable is a Big-O, an invariant, a memory-ordering argument, or a benchmark table → loop-algo. Worked boundary case to put in both bodies: 'shard the queue across N nodes' is loop-design (topology); 'which lock-free queue structure and what are its progress guarantees' is loop-algo.

overlaps.risk: 'It's slow' matches both — a performance regression is a defect, a slow-by-design hot path is a mechanism problem, and users describe them identically.
overlaps.resolution: Split on whether the behavior CHANGED. A regression (it was fast, now it is not; a deploy or commit correlates) is loop-debug — bisect it. Known-correct code that has never been fast enough is loop-algo. Both descriptions carry the pointer; loop-algo's SKILL.md should open by asking 'did this get slower, or was it never fast enough?' and hand off on the first answer.

overlaps.risk: 'Release risk memo' (loop-audit's current description) and 'release checklist / go-no-go' (loop-ship) both fire on 'is this release safe?'.
overlaps.resolution: Split on direction in time. loop-audit is backward-looking over a diff — what is in it, what it touches, how risky, is it covered. loop-ship is forward-looking over a rollout — how it reaches prod, at what ramp, behind what flag, backing out how. loop-ship CONSUMES loop-audit's memo as its go/no-go input, which makes the dependency explicit rather than competitive. Both descriptions gain the pointer (done).

overlaps.risk: 'Add Stripe' spans both: choosing Stripe is scout, wiring Stripe is integrate.
overlaps.resolution: Sequential handoff on a hard boundary: loop-scout terminates at a named recommendation and writes no integration code; loop-integrate begins with the provider already named and never re-litigates the choice. When the user names a specific provider in the request, that is the signal the scout phase is already done — state this in loop-integrate's SKILL.md §1.

overlaps.risk: loop-design/references/api-design.md owns idempotency keys, versioning, error envelopes, and retries — the same vocabulary as loop-integrate's declared scope.
overlaps.resolution: Split on direction of the contract: loop-design owns the API this system PUBLISHES (it writes the spec); loop-integrate owns the API this system CONSUMES (it obeys someone else's spec and defends against it). Idempotency appears in both legitimately but as different obligations — design requires callers to send a key, integrate requires this system to send one. Add a one-line note to api-design.md pointing consumer-side concerns at loop-integrate.

overlaps.risk: 'Contract tests' is named in loop-integrate's scope but authoring tests is loop-test's job.
overlaps.resolution: loop-integrate SPECIFIES the contract (which interactions, which provider states, which pact) and loop-test AUTHORS the files in the repo's stack — the same delegation loop-debug already uses for regression tests. loop-integrate must not hand-roll test files in a framework the repo does not use.

overlaps.risk: Benchmark-driven validation (loop-algo) vs verifying tests run correctly (loop-test) — both are 'write something that runs the code and reports'.
overlaps.resolution: Split on the assertion type: pass/fail correctness assertion → loop-test; a measured distribution compared against a baseline → loop-algo. loop-algo owns benchmark methodology (warmup, variance, statistical significance, what a 5% delta means); loop-test owns everything with an expected value.

overlaps.risk: Pre-existing and already mitigated by loop-audit's pointer, but loop-review's current description contains the bare word 'audit' ('run a security scan or audit'), which fires on 'audit this PR'.
overlaps.resolution: Make the pointer bidirectional. loop-audit already says 'for defects, use loop-review'; loop-review must gain 'for a change-impact and release-risk report rather than a defect hunt, use loop-audit'. Narrow the bare 'audit' to 'security review' in loop-review's trigger list (done in the rewrite).

overlaps.risk: 'Why is this broken?' vs 'find what's wrong with this code' — both are defect-finding.
overlaps.resolution: Split on evidence source: loop-debug requires an OBSERVED failure (a trace, a red test, a reproduction); loop-review works from reading source with no failure in hand. If the user can paste a stack trace, it is loop-debug. Pre-existing and mild, but with 18 skills the pointer should be explicit in both.

overlaps.risk: Pre-existing. 'Orchestrate' appears verbatim in both current descriptions; loop-engine's opens with 'Orchestrate a task…' and loop-orchestrate's with 'Plan and orchestrate…'.
overlaps.resolution: Remove 'orchestrate' as loop-engine's leading verb — it authors and EXECUTES a script (done in the rewrite). loop-orchestrate PLANS and produces a DAG it never runs. Rule of thumb for the descriptions: one project with phases → orchestrate; one task now → engine.

overlaps.risk: A runbook is a document, so loop-docs' 'how-to guide' trigger will catch 'write a runbook for the disk-full alert'.
overlaps.resolution: Split on executor: loop-docs writes for a HUMAN READER seeking understanding (Diataxis); loop-operate writes runbooks whose steps are EXECUTED, possibly unattended, and which must be deterministic, idempotent, and testable. A runbook is an operational artifact that happens to be markdown, not documentation. loop-docs' description gains the pointer (done).

overlaps.risk: 'Write the postmortem' matches loop-docs' documentation triggers.
overlaps.resolution: Postmortems and correction-of-error documents belong to loop-incident, which owns the timeline data and the blameless-analysis method; loop-docs may be delegated the final prose pass but is not the entry point. Pointer added to loop-docs' description.

overlaps.risk: Pre-existing. loop-research's 'compare options with citations' overlaps loop-scout's candidate evaluation.
overlaps.resolution: Already correctly composed — loop-scout §2 delegates its searching to loop-research. Make it explicit in loop-research's description ('for a build-vs-buy decision about something the user is about to build, use loop-scout, which delegates its searching here') so the composition direction is visible at selection time.

overlaps.risk: Both change code inside a component; 'make this cleaner and faster' matches both.
overlaps.resolution: Split on behavior preservation. loop-pattern's diffs are behavior-preserving by definition (a refactoring that changes behavior is a bug). loop-algo deliberately changes the performance profile and sometimes the semantics (ordering, fairness, memory visibility). If the test suite should pass unchanged before and after, it is loop-pattern.

overlaps.risk: Both configure automated recurring behavior; loop-harness/references/automation-loops.md covers Routines and scheduled tasks, and loop-operate covers self-healing runbooks on a schedule.
overlaps.resolution: Split on subject: loop-harness configures what CLAUDE may do (permissions, hooks, MCP, schedulers); loop-operate configures what the SERVICE does when unhealthy. A self-healing runbook may be deployed via a mechanism loop-harness set up — that is composition, and the pointer in loop-harness' description ('the subject is Claude's own configuration, not the product's runtime') keeps it one-directional.

overlaps.risk: Both configure Claude Code itself, so 'set up Claude for this project' plausibly matches either.
overlaps.resolution: Split on what changes: loop-harness changes what Claude is PERMITTED to do (permissions, hooks, MCP, schedules); loop-skill changes what Claude KNOWS HOW to do (a capability). A skill may be deployed via a harness loop-harness set up — that is composition, and the pointer is one-directional.

overlaps.risk: A SKILL.md is markdown, so 'write the docs for this skill' will catch loop-docs' how-to trigger.
overlaps.resolution: Split on the artifact and its contract: loop-docs writes for a HUMAN READER seeking understanding (Diataxis); loop-skill emits a directory that must pass scripts/validate.mjs and whose description field is machine-consumed at selection time. A SKILL.md is an executable contract that happens to be markdown.

overlaps.risk: loop-design/references/frontend.md already owns frontend performance, so 'make the UI faster/smoother' plausibly matches both.
overlaps.resolution: Split PAGE-LOADING performance (loop-design: rendering strategy, bundle budget, LCP/INP/CLS targets, caching) from PER-ANIMATION FRAME COST (loop-frontend: compositor-only properties, FLIP, will-change hygiene). Field test: 'the page takes 4s to appear' is loop-design; 'the drawer stutters when it opens' is loop-frontend. This is the weakest of the four boundaries and both files must say so plainly rather than pretend it is crisp.

overlaps.risk: 'Should I use anime.js?' reads as a library-selection question, which is loop-scout's territory.
overlaps.resolution: loop-frontend walks its own escalation ladder (CSS transition -> keyframes -> View Transitions -> scroll-driven -> WAAPI -> library) and answers 'does THIS motion need a library, and which rung is it?' — most often 'no library'. A project-wide adoption evaluation with criteria, a winner and a runner-up is loop-scout, which loop-frontend hands off to.

overlaps.risk: Both edit component files in a frontend codebase.
overlaps.resolution: Split on what a screenshot can see: loop-pattern's output is a behaviour-preserving refactor backed by tests that a screenshot cannot distinguish; loop-frontend's output is visible by definition and no unit test catches its regression. If both touch one file, loop-pattern decides where the component boundary goes and loop-frontend decides what crosses it in 240ms.

overlaps.risk: loop-engine owns pipeline/parallel/loop shapes and its harness policies (H3 schemas, H7 isolation) already touch state discipline at the single-result scale; a state contract could be read as engine policy.
overlaps.resolution: Checkable question: is the defect in the SHAPE of the run (which stages, which barriers, when to stop) or in the INFORMATION crossing a boundary (what fields, which merge rule, what survives compaction)? Shape → loop-engine; information → loop-context. loop-engine's H3 stays: it governs one agent's return; loop-context governs what accumulates across returns.

overlaps.risk: 'Agent memory' colloquially covers both Claude's memory-dir configuration (harness) and runtime context handling (this skill).
overlaps.resolution: Checkable question: does the fix land in .claude/settings.json, hooks, or MCP config (loop-harness) or in how prompts/state are assembled at runtime (loop-context)?

overlaps.risk: Bi-temporal/supersession vocabulary is shared with database data-modeling.
overlaps.resolution: Checkable question: is the store the PRODUCT's (users query it) or the AGENT's (the model queries it mid-run)? Product → loop-design; agent → loop-context.

overlaps.risk: Both produce architecture artifacts (C4 diagrams, ADRs). A user saying 'document the architecture' of an existing repo could match either; loop-design also owns ADR practice and the adr-template.
overlaps.resolution: Checkable question: is the architecture being read out of code that already runs, or decided for code not yet written? Recovery of as-built structure and reverse-engineered ADRs (status: recovered, confidence-graded) is loop-comprehend; forward decisions and new ADRs are loop-design. A recovery that concludes 'this should change' ends at the finding and hands the recovered ADR to loop-design as context; the new ADR supersedes the recovered one. Pointers on both sides.

overlaps.risk: 'Explain this codebase' and 'document this codebase' are adjacent triggers. loop-docs verifies claims against source too, so both skills read code and emit prose.
overlaps.resolution: Checkable question: is the deliverable a maintained document the repo keeps (README, guide, numbered ADR set — loop-docs), or a dated, evidence-anchored answer/dossier stamped with the commit it describes (loop-comprehend)? loop-comprehend produces the understanding and hands anything meant to live longer than a snapshot to loop-docs, whose rot catalogue owns keeping it true. Pointers on both sides.

overlaps.risk: Both map code and trace blast radius; 'what does this touch' fires near both.
overlaps.resolution: Checkable question: is the subject a specific change set (diff, PR, commit range, release) or the codebase as it stands? A change set is loop-audit; the standing system is loop-comprehend. A comprehension map is legitimate input to an audit, never its substitute. Pointers on both sides.

overlaps.risk: Feature tracing and defect localization use the same moves (both-ends anchoring, runtime evidence).
overlaps.resolution: Checkable question: is there one observed defective behavior to explain? Yes is loop-debug (reproduce, localize, fix); no — the behavior is correct and merely opaque — is loop-comprehend. A trace that uncovers a defect hands its reproduction to loop-debug as a head start. Pointer carried on loop-comprehend's side; loop-debug's description already scopes itself to observed failures.

overlaps.risk: loop-autopilot/references/comprehension-rot.md uses the word 'comprehension' for the human's decaying understanding of an autonomous loop's merges.
overlaps.resolution: Different subject entirely: comprehension-rot is a sampling digest inside a standing automation loop (subject: the loop's merge stream); loop-comprehend is on-demand understanding of a codebase (subject: the code). No trigger phrase collision found; no description change needed on either side.

overlaps.risk: Both sit above the domain skills and decide what runs where; 'figure out how to tackle this' plausibly fires either.
overlaps.resolution: Checkable question: can the user name the job and its deliverable? Named and scoped, wanting a phased plan with model routing and a cost ledger → loop-orchestrate. Unnamed — the question is which skill or job this even is → loop-guide, whose deliverable is a routing verdict, not a DAG. Guide escalates named multi-phase jobs to orchestrate; orchestrate assumes the job arrives named. Pointers on both sides.

overlaps.risk: A guide chain and a conducted project look alike from outside: multiple skills invoked in order with artifacts crossing between them.
overlaps.resolution: Checkable question: does the execution need gates, repair rounds, and a ledger? A 2–4 hop chain with per-boundary handoff checks is loop-guide conduction; brief-to-v1, or any chain reaching ~5 hops, is loop-build — guide's dispatch.md carries the tripwire and hands over completed hops as the brief. Pointers on both sides.

overlaps.risk: 'Heimdall can't do X' arrives at the front door and could read as a routing failure.
overlaps.resolution: Checkable question: does any existing skill's boundary contain the ask? Yes → route to it; no → the gap itself is the finding, escalated to loop-skill as a candidate charter. Guide never authors. Pointers on both sides.

descriptionRewrites.currentDescription: Diagnose and fix bugs with a reproduce to localize to root-cause to fix method. Drives hypothesis-driven debugging and adds a regression test once fixed.
descriptionRewrites.newDescription: Find the root cause of a specific defective behavior and fix it, using reproduce, localize, hypothesize, eliminate, minimal fix, regression test. Use when the user reports a bug, a failing test, an exception or stack trace, a crash, or unexpected behavior in code they can run, and asks why it happens or how to fix it. Drives hypothesis-driven elimination and delegates the regression test to loop-test. For a production service that is currently degraded or down with users affected, use loop-incident first, which mitigates and hands the root cause back here. For code that is correct but too slow or memory-hungry by design, use loop-algo. For a defect found by reading code rather than by observing a failure, use loop-review.
descriptionRewrites.why: The current wording ('a crash', 'unexpected behavior', 'why something is broken') is exactly what a user types during an outage, so it will out-compete loop-incident on the trigger that matters most and start bisecting while the service is down. Adds the three highest-risk pointers (incident, algo, review) and constrains the subject to code the user can run.

descriptionRewrites.currentDescription: Design software systems and architecture: architecture-style selection, API design, backend and data modeling, frontend performance, deployment strategy, and non-functional requirements. Use when the user asks to design a system or architecture, choose an architecture pattern, design an API, plan a deployment or rollout strategy, optimize frontend performance, model backend data, or record architecture decisions (ADRs) and C4 diagrams.
descriptionRewrites.newDescription: Design software systems and architecture: architecture-style selection, API design, backend and data modeling, frontend performance, and turning non-functional requirements into numbers and SLO targets. Use when the user asks to design a system or architecture, choose an architecture pattern, design an API this system exposes, model backend data, pick a consistency policy, optimize frontend performance, set NFR or capacity targets, or record architecture decisions as ADRs and C4 diagrams. Works at component granularity on a system not yet built. For executing a release or choosing a rollout strategy for a system already running, use loop-ship. For measuring and alerting on the SLOs of a live service, use loop-operate. For the algorithm inside one component, use loop-algo.
descriptionRewrites.why: 'Deployment strategy' and 'plan a deployment or rollout strategy' are loop-ship's core triggers and must leave loop-design's description entirely, or the two skills compete for every release question. Also disambiguates API direction (exposed vs consumed) against loop-integrate, marks the design-time/run-time seam against loop-operate, and marks granularity against loop-algo.

descriptionRewrites.currentDescription: Review code for security vulnerabilities and quality issues using OWASP Top 10, CWE Top 25, and ASVS standards. Use when the user asks to review code, run a security scan or audit, check for vulnerabilities, do a code-quality or best-practices review, or assess a diff, PR, or repo for injection, auth, crypto, secrets, SSRF, or dependency risks.
descriptionRewrites.newDescription: Review code for security vulnerabilities and quality defects using OWASP Top 10, CWE Top 25, and ASVS, and report them without changing the code. Use when the user asks to review code, scan for vulnerabilities, do a security or code-quality review, or assess a diff, PR, or repo for injection, auth, crypto, secrets, SSRF, or dependency risk. Reports HIGH and MEDIUM findings at confidence at or above 0.8; it judges, it does not refactor. For applying the refactoring that fixes a reported smell, use loop-pattern. For a change-impact and release-risk report rather than a defect hunt, use loop-audit. For diagnosing a failure that was actually observed at runtime, use loop-debug.
descriptionRewrites.why: 'It judges, it does not refactor' is the single clause that keeps 'clean up this code' out of loop-review and in loop-pattern. Drops the bare word 'audit' that collides with loop-audit, and makes loop-audit's existing one-way pointer bidirectional as required at 18 skills.

descriptionRewrites.currentDescription: Find existing frameworks, libraries, tools, or standards that already solve a problem before building it from scratch — a prior-art and build-vs-buy check that prevents reinventing the wheel and over-engineering. Use when the user is about to build a component, feature, or system, asks whether to build or adopt an existing solution, wants to avoid reinventing something, asks whether a library or framework exists for a need, or is scoping work that likely has established solutions.
descriptionRewrites.newDescription: Find existing frameworks, libraries, tools, services, or standards that already solve a problem before building it from scratch, a prior-art and build-vs-buy check that prevents reinventing the wheel. Use when the user is about to build a component or feature, asks whether to build or adopt an existing solution, asks whether a library exists for a need, or is choosing between candidate dependencies. Ends at a decision: reuse, adapt, or build, naming the candidate and the runner-up. For using a framework already in the project idiomatically, use loop-pattern. For wiring up a chosen third-party platform or API, use loop-integrate. For a question that needs cited evidence rather than a build-vs-buy decision, use loop-research.
descriptionRewrites.why: 'Ends at a decision' plus the loop-pattern and loop-integrate pointers install the not-yet-adopted / already-a-dependency / already-chosen boundary that separates scout from the two new skills that flank it on either side of the adoption timeline.

descriptionRewrites.currentDescription: Run an autonomous engineering loop that improves this project — read feedback (GitHub issues, PR comments, CI failures), act on it as draft pull requests with tests, and when there is no feedback, research improvements (market trends, papers, tech-debt scan) and propose them. Use when the user wants to automate project maintenance, set up a self-improving or autonomous engineering loop, continuously triage and act on issues/PRs, or have Claude propose improvements on a schedule. descriptionRewrites.newDescription: Run an autonomous engineering loop over this repository: read feedback (GitHub issues, PR comments, CI failures), act on it as draft pull requests with tests, and when there is no feedback, research improvements and propose them. Use when the user wants to automate repository maintenance, set up a self-improving engineering loop, continuously triage issues and PRs, or have Claude propose code improvements on a schedule. The subject is the codebase and the output is a draft PR; it composes the plugin's other skills, proposes only, and never merges. For running and self-healing a live production service rather than improving a repo, use loop-operate. For a single one-off orchestrated job rather than a standing loop, use loop-orchestrate.
descriptionRewrites.why: 'This project' is ambiguous once loop-operate exists — a running service is also 'this project'. Pinning the subject to the repository and the output to a draft PR is the one statement that separates two skills which are otherwise both 'an autonomous loop with an autonomy dial'.

descriptionRewrites.currentDescription: Audit a set of code changes and produce an impact and risk report. For finding security or quality defects to fix, use loop-review instead.
descriptionRewrites.newDescription: Audit a set of code changes and produce an impact and risk report: classify each change, trace blast radius, rate risk, and check test coverage. Use when the user asks to audit a diff, PR, release, or commit range, summarize what changed, assess impact or blast radius, check whether changes are covered by tests, or produce a change report or release risk memo. Reports on a change set that already exists; it neither hunts defects nor plans the rollout. For finding security or quality defects to fix, use loop-review instead. For planning how the release reaches production and how it rolls back, use loop-ship.
descriptionRewrites.why: 'Release risk memo' now collides head-on with loop-ship's go/no-go. Adds the backward-looking framing and the loop-ship pointer while keeping the existing loop-review pointer, which is the house-style exemplar for this pattern.

descriptionRewrites.currentDescription: Write and repair automated tests: design cases, match the project test framework, and verify tests run and fail for the right reason. Use when the user asks to write, add, generate, or fix tests, improve coverage, add a regression test for a bug, or set up testing for a module. Matches the repo existing test stack and conventions.
descriptionRewrites.newDescription: Write and repair automated correctness tests: design cases, match the project's test framework and conventions, and verify each test runs and fails for the right reason before it passes. Use when the user asks to write, add, generate, or fix tests, improve coverage, add a regression test for a bug, or set up testing for a module. Covers happy-path, edge, error, and property-based cases. For performance benchmarks and complexity validation, use loop-algo. For contract tests against a third-party provider, use loop-integrate, which specifies the contract this skill then authors. For finding the bug a regression test should lock in, use loop-debug.
descriptionRewrites.why: Three new skills now name test-shaped artifacts (loop-algo benchmarks, loop-integrate contract tests, loop-incident repro harnesses). Narrowing to 'correctness tests' and naming the two delegations keeps loop-test the authoring service for all of them instead of a competitor.

descriptionRewrites.currentDescription: Write and maintain technical documentation: READMEs, API references, docstrings, guides, and ADRs. Follows the Diataxis doc-type model and matches repo conventions.
descriptionRewrites.newDescription: Write and maintain technical documentation: READMEs, API references, docstrings, guides, and ADR prose, verifying every claim against the source. Follows the Diataxis doc-type model and matches repo conventions. For deciding the architecture an ADR records, use loop-design. For writing a runbook an operator or automated loop executes, use loop-operate. For an incident postmortem or correction-of-error, use loop-incident.
descriptionRewrites.why: Runbooks and postmortems are markdown, so loop-docs' 'how-to guide' trigger would capture both of loop-operate's and loop-incident's signature deliverables. The pointers encode the human-reader vs executed-artifact split.

descriptionRewrites.currentDescription: Research a topic across multiple sources with adversarial fact-checking and a cited synthesis. descriptionRewrites.newDescription: Research a question across multiple sources with adversarial fact-checking and a cited synthesis. Every claim carries a source. For a build-vs-buy or prior-art decision about something the user is about to build, use loop-scout, which delegates its searching here.
descriptionRewrites.why: 'Compare options with citations' is indistinguishable from loop-scout's candidate evaluation at selection time. Naming the composition direction ('which delegates its searching here') resolves it without narrowing loop-research's legitimate scope.

descriptionRewrites.currentDescription: Plan and orchestrate multi-agent project work: decompose a project into a task DAG, choose pipeline or parallel workflow shapes, and assign the right Claude model and effort tier to each task (right model for the right job). descriptionRewrites.newDescription: Plan multi-agent project work: decompose a project into a typed task DAG, choose pipeline or parallel shapes per phase, route the right Claude model and effort tier to each task, and produce a cost ledger. descriptionRewrites.newDescription: Author and execute a multi-agent Workflow script (pipeline, parallel with an earned barrier, or a guarded loop) governed by the harness and loop engineering policies and a pluggable lifecycle framework (default AIDLC). This is the execution engine every other skill's templates target. For decomposing a whole project into a phased DAG with model routing before execution, use loop-orchestrate.

The subject is Claude's own configuration, not the product's runtime. For operating the deployed service the repo produces, use loop-operate. For the content of the autonomous loop the harness schedules, use loop-autopilot.

Pinning the subject to Claude's own configuration is the one sentence that keeps 'automate this check every 5 minutes' routed correctly depending on whether the check runs against the repo or against production.

descriptionRewrites.currentDescription: (new in v1.0.0 — no SKILL.md exists yet; plan scope line: 'Applies patterns/idioms/refactorings. GoF, Fowler Refactoring 2e, SOLID, language style guides, idiomatic framework use. Distinct from loop-review, which only judges.')

For a declared outage affecting users right now, use loop-incident. For choosing SLO targets for a system not yet built, use loop-design. For automating improvements to a repository rather than a running service, use loop-autopilot.
descriptionRewrites.why: The most contested description in the set — it must fend off loop-incident (episodic vs steady state), loop-design (which owns SLO target-setting today in nfr.md), and loop-autopilot (the other autonomous loop). 'In steady state' and 'running/live service' are the two phrases doing that work.

verdict:
All 18 boundaries hold, but two of them hold only conditionally, and shipping v1.0.0 without meeting those conditions would produce exactly the failure the plan's Open Risk #1 predicts.

CONDITION 1 (blocking, loop-ship and loop-operate). loop-design does not merely overlap the two new operational skills — it already CONTAINS them. `loop-design/references/deployment.md` is 149 lines covering rolling/blue-green/canary mechanics and failure modes, the risk-to-strategy table, the four feature-flag kinds, expand-contract migrations, IaC, CI/CD gating, tested rollback, and the complete DORA scorecard: that is 100% of loop-ship's declared scope, already written, already shipped in v0.4.0. `loop-design/references/nfr.md` likewise already owns SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting, RED/USE/golden signals, and OpenTelemetry — the core of loop-operate. Description surgery alone cannot fix this; two skills cannot share one body of knowledge and be selected reliably. Phase 2 must MOVE the content: deployment.md out of loop-design into loop-ship (split into rollout-strategies.md / migrations.md / dora.md, leaving a ~15-line design-time ADR stub plus pointer), and nfr.md's SLO-measurement and observability sections into loop-operate (leaving the target-setting half, availability math, RTO/RPO, scalability, and cost behind). The seam is checkable: if answering the question requires reading a live metric or executing a deploy, it is not loop-design. If Construction declines the migration, do NOT ship loop-ship as a separate skill — fold it back into loop-design step 6, because it would otherwise be a verbatim duplicate.

CONDITION 2 (non-blocking, loop-autopilot and loop-operate). Both carry an autonomy ladder. Two definitions will drift within one release. Promote the OBSERVE-to-SCALE ladder to a single home (recommend `loop-engine/references/autonomy-ladder.md`) and have both skills cite it; neither redefines it. Relatedly, loop-autopilot's `canary-merge.workflow.js` should cite loop-ship for the rollout mechanism and loop-operate for the SLO gate rather than restating either.

NO MERGE IS RECOMMENDED — but one pair is on probation. loop-incident vs loop-operate is the thinnest boundary in the 18. It is separable today only because of a single checkable predicate: does a runbook exist for this condition AND does executing it restore the SLI? Yes means loop-operate (steady state, automated, known); no or beyond-scope means loop-incident (declared, coordinated, novel). That predicate must be the FIRST sentence of both SKILL.md bodies, not buried in a reference. Give the Phase 2 verify-sweep an explicit merge tripwire: if either skill's body ends up spending more than roughly 30% of its length restating the other's phase, they are not genuinely separable and should be merged into loop-operate with an 'incident mode' section. One honest skill beats two that fight for the same trigger.

The five clusters named in the brief resolve as follows. (a) The detect/mitigate/root-cause/redeploy chain holds on four distinct predicates — runbook-covered vs not (operate/incident), service restored vs not (incident/debug), defect vs release (debug/ship), rollout in flight vs baked (ship/operate) — provided loop-debug's description surrenders its outage-shaped trigger phrases, which the rewrite does. (b) loop-review vs loop-pattern holds cleanly on the artifact produced: findings list vs diff. (c) loop-scout vs loop-pattern holds on a fact both can check in one command — does answering this add a line to the dependency manifest. (d) loop-design vs loop-algo vs loop-ship holds on granularity and phase (boxes vs Big-O vs rollout), once Condition 1 is met. (e) loop-autopilot vs loop-operate holds on subject (repository vs running service) and output (draft PR vs mitigated SLI), once Condition 2 is met.

Two cross-cutting notes for Construction. First, every description in the matrix now carries at least one 'use X instead when Y' pointer and several carry three; that redundancy is deliberate, because selection happens on the description alone, before any body is read. Second, only loop-engine and loop-orchestrate currently declare `argument-hint` in frontmatter — the `mode-propagate` task should add it to the other ten alongside `--mode`, since a skill with no argument-hint gives the model no shape cue at invocation time.
